scope: Calibration corpus of real works at: 60th Venice Biennale 2024 (Foreigners Everywhere: Nucleo Contemporaneo, Nucleo Storico, national pavilions); Whitney Biennial 2024 and 2026; Barbican Unravel (2024); Tate Modern Hyundai Commission 2023, 2024, 2025; Carnegie International 2022; Made in L.A. 2025 (exhibition notes only). Hayward Gallery and Serpentine shows were searched (Kapoor, Doig House of Music, Halsey Emajendat) but no work records were written for them. Descriptions are paraphrased from the reviews and museum pages listed in each record; where a field was not stated in a source it is null.

exhibitions.name: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
exhibitions.artistic_director: Adriano Pedrosa (artistic director of MASP, Sao Paulo)
exhibitions.title_metaphor: Title taken from a neon series by the collective Claire Fontaine (running since 2004, in many languages), which riffs on a Turin anti-racist collective's slogan. Pedrosa extends 'foreigner' to everyone: wherever you are, deep down you are a foreigner. It names four groups the show centres: queer artists, outsider artists, folk artists and Indigenous artists, plus migrants and diaspora artists. He also cites Freud's Unheimlich (the strange that is also familiar) and Edward Said's Culture and Imperialism.
sections: Nucleo Contemporaneo (Giardini Central Pavilion and Arsenale)
Nucleo Storico: Italians Everywhere (Arsenale, hung on Lina Bo Bardi glass easels)
Disobedience Archive (Marco Scotini, Arsenale film archive)
critic_notes: Most critics agreed the main show reads like a museum exhibition: sparse hangs, many dead artists (more than half of the 331 per one count), a lot of painting and textile, few screens or digital works.
A recurring wall-label formula marked artists as exhibiting at the Biennale for the first time. Critics saw this as the show's main rhetorical device and its 'historical debt' gesture.

Nucleo Storico portrait rooms were called the weakest section: about 100 single works by 100 artists, uneven, some 'ropey', hung salon-style in grey rooms. The Abstractions room was praised for musical cross-resonances. Italians Everywhere on Lina Bo Bardi glass easels was widely admired as the show's best display idea.
Textiles were noted as a through-line in the older work (Wenger, Abad, de Amaral, Bordadoras de Isla Negra), with many critics saying younger fibre artists were under-represented.

ArtReview (Charlesworth) and others argued that platforming minoritised groups can only give symbolic recognition and that the curatorial rhetoric was benign cosmopolitanism. Several called intro texts generic artspeak.

Dean Kissick (Harper's, 'The Painted Protest', Dec 2024) argued that biennials now offer progressive content in conservative forms (naive scenes of everyday life, traditional pottery, carving, dyed cloth, portraits of identity), with wall texts that assign political meaning the object cannot show. He singled out Louis Fratino as modernist pastiche, and praised the Yahuarcani painters, Susanne Wenger and Xiyadie as truly strange; he also praised Bartolini's Italian Pavilion as a non-message utopian space.

Hyperallergic (Vartanian) called neon-phrase works like Claire Fontaine's hollow and over-intellectualised; criticised the Disobedience Archive's tiny-screen design as a wasted room; praised Pablo Delano but said his archive-room felt like a rabbit hole in this context.

Art in America (Watlington) said the something-for-everyone approach abolishes hierarchy and makes it hard to judge; a few living artists (Toranzo Jaeger, Halsey) were read as sceptical of the inclusion on offer.

National pavilions were a mixed bag. Strong reception for Australia (Moore, Golden Lion), Japan (Mohri), Italy (Bartolini), Germany (long queues), Netherlands (cocoa smell, CATPC) and the UK (Akomfrah, five hours long, too much to take in). FT critic called many western pavilions lacklustre and one-dimensional.

Golden Lion for best participant: Mataaho Collective (Takapau). Golden Lion for national participation: Australia. Lifetime Golden Lion included Nil Yalter. Silver Lion for a promising young artist: Karimah Ashadu.

exhibitions.name: Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing
exhibitions.title_metaphor: Title borrowed from a U2 song (jaunty lyric: you're the real thing, even better than the real thing). The curatorial idea: the real, the authentic and the copy; a 'dissonant chorus' of bodies that shapeshift freely in physical and virtual space; artists who resist being flattened or essentialised by identity categories. Onli framed the moment as as feverish as the 1990s culture wars.
sections: Floors 5 and 6 plus lobby, stairwell and terraces
Film and performance programmes (29 of the participants)
Hyundai Terrace Commission (Torkwase Dyson), north roof deck
critic_notes: Widely read as quiet, cool, slow-burn and light on loud political statements, with heavy emphasis on bodies in flux, absent bodies (architecture, fabric and objects standing in for body parts) and conceptual work.
ARTnews (Greenberger) called it 'blazing' and said it heralds a new kind of body art made of cast, scanned or stand-in forms; many works are clean, pale and slick.

ArtReview noted minimalist restraint and an intimate closed plan, more harmony than 'dissonance'; Brooklyn Rail praised the many small acts of care, but said socially engaged group projects can trade emotion for administration.
The Art Newspaper saw resonant pairings across rooms (for example Pusey's paintings against Weston's smoked glass) and a show that rewards close looking.
Several reviewers noted that the show hardly mentioned Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan or the Congo apart from one flickering neon (DinéYazhi, hidden 'Free Palestine').

Harper's (Kissick) used the Whitney as an example of the wall-text problem: a smoked-glass ceiling, an upside-down tipi, a field walk with a dowsing rod, found lobster traps on a salt rope, each carrying a long decolonial or refusal claim that the object itself cannot show.

Recurring forms: ceramic, cast, 3D-printed, crocheted, found-object assemblage, unfixed photographic film, player piano, text neon, AI model, film installations with beds or cushions. Painting was fewer than expected.

exhibitions.name: Whitney Biennial 2026
exhibitions.title_metaphor: Untitled and deliberately themeless. The curators invited artists from places touched by US military or political power (Afghanistan, Chile, Iraq, Okinawa, Palestine, the Philippines, Puerto Rico, Vietnam) and framed US presence as 'residues of empire' handled abstractly, poetically or ambivalently. Staged in the year of the US 250th anniversary. Catalogue essay language: relationality, infrastructure, entanglements, kinships (including animal and plant kin).
sections: Fifth floor: bodies, families, kinship, mourning and altars
Sixth floor: infrastructure, surveillance, cities, systems
critic_notes: A mood of grief and shrines: Hyperallergic wrote that mourning, shrines and grief ran through both floors. The Week summarised critics as saying the show is light on message and big on feelings, with small-scale work halfway between sculpture and talisman.

ArtReview (Wu): the show suits the aesthetic categories 'cute, zany, interesting' (after Sianne Ngai) better than the social or political; art as knock-off, like Santiago's 'Sanhattan' versus Manhattan.

e-flux (Lossin): the sixth floor was articulate and legible; the fifth floor was variable and vague, and the press-release vocabulary ('transition', 'tenderness', 'mood and texture') evaded politics. Hyperallergic (Bishara) said the show shies away from the moment; D'Souza found it terrific in installation, beautiful and mournful but not weird.
Frieze headline: an underwhelming show for overwhelming times. Fine Art Globe: bold and messy, no organising principle.

Historical or rediscovered artists carried much of the force: Agosto Machado's altars, Carmen de Monteflores, Kimowan Metchewais, Jose Maceda. Interspecies work (dog toys, insects, frogs and moles in circuit diagrams) was a visible new trope. AI, surveillance and games appeared (Castaneda, Ruiz, Blas, Citarella).

exhibitions.name: Unravel: The Power and Politics of Textiles in Art
exhibitions.artistic_director: Lotte Johnson and Wells Fray-Smith (curators; assistant curator Diego Chocano); Barbican Art Gallery with Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam
exhibitions.title_metaphor: 'Unravel' plays on thread and undoing. The thesis: textiles were marginalised as feminine craft, and the marginalisation of the medium tracks the marginalisation of people by gender, race, geography and wealth; stitching, weaving, braiding, beading and knotting become tools of resistance. Starts in the 1960s with fibre art coming off the wall into three dimensions.
critic_notes: Time Out said that insisting every work 'undermines power' draws attention to how overblown the language is, that the show treats Abakanowicz and Margolles as serving one purpose, and that it hangs together poorly despite strong pieces.

Kissick (Harper's) called it a liberal-orthodoxy show in traditional methods and recognisable aesthetics that could have been made fifty years earlier. He linked it to the Venice Biennale as a shared 'nostalgic turn to history'.
Hackney Citizen and others praised its breadth: quilts, silk collage, tapestry, hanging wool, bandages, blood, border-patrol uniforms.

The show was hit by withdrawals and statements after the Barbican refused to host an LRB lecture series; empty spaces and pinned letters became part of the display (Vicuña stayed in and added a letter; Yee I-Lann added an office table with the LRB issue).

The Conversation argued the textile revival is driven by feminist art history, social movements, biennials and fairs, and the commercial convenience of textiles (easier to ship and install than paintings).

exhibitions.name: Hyundai Commission, Tate Modern Turbine Hall 2023
exhibitions.artistic_director: El Anatsui; curators Osei Bonsu and Dina Akhamadeeva (as reported)
exhibitions.title_metaphor: Behind the Red Moon: staged as three acts (sail/moon, world, wall) about the Atlantic trade triangle in rum, sugar and people, and the Notsie wall in Ewe history. The Turbine Hall is imagined as a ship.
critic_notes: Reviewers called it glorious and monumental; some said acts one and three overpower the middle act.

exhibitions.name: Hyundai Commission, Tate Modern Turbine Hall 2024
exhibitions.artistic_director: Mire Lee; curated by Alvin Li with Bilal Akkouche
exhibitions.title_metaphor: Open Wound: the building reimagined as the inside of a body and a living factory; the turbine as 'an open wound that never closes'; the time of decline; soft organic forms against rigid mechanical systems.
critic_notes: The Tate texts frame the work through coal-miner pit-head baths, textile manufacture and the Bankside power station, and ask what the museum 'generates' today.

exhibitions.name: Hyundai Commission, Tate Modern Turbine Hall 2025
exhibitions.artistic_director: Máret Ánne Sara; curated by Helen O'Malley and Hannah Gorlizki
exhibitions.title_metaphor: Goavve-Geabbil: 'goavvi' is the Sami word for an ice crust that forms on snow after melt and refreeze and starves reindeer; 'geabbil' stands for adaptability and mutual support. Energy is framed as a sacred life-force, not a resource.
critic_notes: Reviews were mixed. Some critics called the work tame and quiet rather than spectacular; Hyperallergic saw a useful move: the structure and wall texts argue for Indigenous knowledge as hard science, not just 'wisdom'.

exhibitions.name: 58th Carnegie International: Is it morning for you yet?
exhibitions.artistic_director: Sohrab Mohebbi (curator) with Ryan Inouye and Talia Heiman
exhibitions.title_metaphor: Title is a Kaqchikel Maya greeting ('good morning'). The show measures the US geopolitical footprint since 1945 through artists from places affected by US power, with an emphasis on political abstraction.
sections: Four mini-exhibitions: Museo de la Solidaridad Salvador Allende; Fereydoun Ave and Laal collection (Iran); Dogma Collection (Vietnam, 1975); Zahia Rahmani, Seismography of Struggle
Commissions beyond the museum (mural in Hill District, billboards on Route 28)
critic_notes: Brooklyn Rail: nearly everything that looks like art-for-art's-sake carries political meaning only through labels and materials. Art in America: sharp, historically grounded curatorial argument built on abstraction. Artnet: did little to stand out on the biennial circuit. Counts of participants vary by source (about 80 collectives, institutions and estates vs more than 100 participants).

exhibitions.name: Made in L.A. 2025 (Hammer Museum)
exhibitions.title_metaphor: Biennial of artists practising in the Los Angeles area; the curators describe a 'no-methodology methodology' and a city that is 'neither myth nor monolith'. A Frank Lloyd Wright quote about everything loose rolling to Los Angeles is stencilled on one wall.
sections: Three floors, indoor and outdoor galleries
critic_notes: ArtReview and Hyperallergic both found the show curatorially scattered, with strong work mainly where artists got their own rooms (Hanna Hur's panels, Na Mira's mirrored two-sided projection, Mike Stoltz's four-channel video, Gabriela Ruiz's screaming-face assemblage with a live surveillance camera, Amanda Ross-Ho's oversized nursing-home door). No works from this show are in the works list because only secondary notes were read in this pass.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.artist_born: Founded 2012 in Aotearoa New Zealand; Maori women's collective (Te Atiawa ki Whakarongotai, Ngati Toa Rangatira and other iwi)
works.title: Takapau
works.medium_line: Woven reflective truck straps
works.what_you_see: A huge lattice of woven reflective cargo straps stretches overhead and crosses the first big room of the Arsenale. It forms a dense, womb-like cradle or canopy. Light makes the straps glow, and a dazzling pattern of shadow falls on walls and floor. Visitors walk under and through it; the scale is architectural.
materials: reflective tape from high-visibility safety gear
claims: The jury described a woven structure that is both a cosmology and a shelter.
The collective says the hi-vis material honours working-class parents and siblings whose labour makes them visible yet invisible.
Scale is a feat of engineering made possible by collective strength.
works.photo_notes: Published views show the strap lattice glowing and throwing a dense pattern of shadows on walls and floor.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.title: kith and kin
works.medium_line: White chalk on black walls; tables with redacted documents; reflective pool
works.what_you_see: Black-painted rooms are covered from floor to ceiling in a hand-chalked family tree, with names and gaps tracing Kamilaroi, Bigambul and British ancestry back 65,000 years. Some entries are racist slurs or colonial names; blank circles mark people who were killed, died of disease or were erased from records. In the centre a black reflective pool sits beneath tables that carry redacted coroners' inquest papers on Indigenous deaths in custody. The doors open and close, flooding the dark room with light.
nonvisual: light: doors that open and close flood the room with daylight
claims: Celebrates First Nations ideas of lineage and connection while exposing trauma and bureaucratic record-keeping.
Links Australia's history to the carceral system from penal colonies to present incarceration rates.
works.photo_notes: Published photos show black walls dense with white chalk handwriting and a central pool.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.title: Come, let me heal your wounds. Let me mend your broken bones
works.medium_line: Darning on medicinally dyed silk
works.what_you_see: Large sheets of silk hang in broad vertical expanses through the room, coloured in warm tones from herbs and spices. Each sheet is deliberately torn, then sutured with darning stitches to mark a place of heritage destroyed by war or terrorism. The newest tears refer to Gaza. Visitors walk between the hangings as they would between curtains.
materials: herb and spice dyes with medicinal properties
nonvisual: scent: not stated; the dyes are medicinal herbs and spices
claims: Each patch of mending represents one cultural site destroyed in conflict.
The medicinal dyes pass on healing knowledge studied in Kerala and with Saudi Indigenous communities.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.artist_born: Group of self-taught women, Isla Negra, Chile; active 1967 to 1980
works.title: Untitled
works.medium_line: Embroidered canvas; natural and synthetic wool
works.what_you_see: A very wide, brightly coloured embroidered wall hanging crowded with scenes of life in a Chilean coastal village: social events and local figures. At nearly eight metres it runs along a wall like a mural. The surface is dense, hand-stitched wool.
claims: Documents daily life and personalities of Isla Negra in the late 1960s and 1970s.
The work was stolen after the 1973 Pinochet takeover of the building and returned in 2019.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.medium_line: Wax-resist batik with cassava-starch paste, indigo-dyed cloth
works.what_you_see: Indigo-blue hangings with staring, wild-eyed figures drawn in resist lines. The figures are stylised archetypes and deities in dense compositions. They hang as tapestries in the Arsenale among other fibre work.
claims: Shows experiments with the Yoruba resist-dye technique adire eleko.
Wenger, a Viennese-trained artist who became a Yoruba priestess, is presented as the foreigner par excellence.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.title: You Have to Blend in before You Stand Out
works.medium_line: Oil, painted batik cloth, sequins, buttons on stitched and padded canvas
works.what_you_see: A large, almost square padded canvas with raised surfaces made by stuffing and stitching (trapunto). It is covered in saturated painted cloth, sequins and buttons. Scenes of urban life from her travels are layered into a graphic composition. In the same show her Filipinas in Hong Kong (1995) depicts the Sunday gatherings of Filipina domestic workers.
claims: Trapunto painting is her own technique, applied to scenes of migrant life and urban belonging.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.artist_born: Guarani ceramicist; birth year not stated
works.title: Untitled (ceramic miniatures)
works.medium_line: Ceramic, small figures
works.what_you_see: Tiny hand-built clay animals set on a plinth or in a vitrine. One is a smiling frog-like creature; another, a creature like an armadillo with an aardvark head, curls up in a protective posture. They are whimsical and small next to the large works around them.
claims: Rodas learned traditional methods from her mother and grandmother and developed an imaginative world of creatures, including a series of musicians.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.venue_room: Outside the Arsenale main building, along the water
works.title: keepers of the krown
works.medium_line: Glass fibre reinforced concrete and mixed media (as listed by the gallery); concrete columns and benches
works.what_you_see: A row of tall white columns in an Egyptian style stand outside the Arsenale near the water. Their capitals are sculpted portraits of friends and neighbours who look down on visitors. The shafts carry relief panels that copy hand-made shop signs from her neighbourhood, plus Egyptian symbols and phrases etched like graffiti. Three white benches echo the decoration.
claims: Fuses ancient Egyptian architecture with the vernacular signs and portraits of South Central Los Angeles, which the artist treats as one continuum of Black culture.
Inscriptions include 'Thou shall not fold' and 'We want a full and complete freedom'.
works.photo_notes: Photographed outdoors outside the Arsenale (photo credit Andrea Avezzu, courtesy artist and Gagosian).

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.title: Prêt-À-Patria
works.medium_line: Fibreglass and steel
works.what_you_see: Three figures in military dress climb in a line towards the ceiling of the Arsenale. A golden flagpole connects them, passing from anus to mouth. A circular red carpet sets the border so visitors cannot get close. From the front the figures look flayed or impaled; from the side they look like a human caterpillar.
claims: The title plays on pret-a-porter and patria, nation as ready-to-wear.
works.photo_notes: Described as hard to photograph from one angle because of the vertical stack and the carpet boundary.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.title: Rage is a Machine in Times of Senselessness
works.medium_line: Multi-canvas polyptych with embroidery
works.dimensions: Mural scale, stepped to a central peak
works.what_you_see: A giant painted polyptych whose panels step up in height to a central peak like a ziggurat. It shows angular car-like machines with exhaust pipes blowing crimson smoke, looping lines like musical staves, and cut-outs of landscape with a gathering of queer women among ferns. Embroidery by the artist's Indigenous relatives is stitched into the canvas. It faces another vast mural at the other end of the Corderie.
claims: The artist calls the hiring of Indigenous family members to embroider 'semiological vandalism' of European painting's preciousness.
references: Frida Kahlo (Viva la Vida, The Two Fridas)

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.artist_born: Puerto Rico connection; birth details not in sources
works.title: The Museum of the Old Colony
works.medium_line: Archive-based conceptual installation
works.what_you_see: A crowded room-sized display that works like a small history museum. It mixes official objects (a Mattel-approved light-skinned Puerto Rican Barbie doll) with photographs (dark-skinned schoolchildren looking at a painting of Abraham Lincoln in San Juan). Everything points to over 500 years of colonial rule since 1493.
claims: Documents repressive Spanish and US acts against Indigenous and Afro-descendant Puerto Ricans.
A critic wrote it felt like a rabbit hole for visitors with limited time.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.artist: Santiago Yahuarcani and Rember Yahuarcani (father and son)
works.artist_born: Uitoto Nation, White Heron clan, Peruvian Amazon
works.medium_line: Santiago: paint on tree bark or paper (light ground); Rember: paint on canvas (black ground)
works.what_you_see: Two sets of enormous, crowded paintings hung as a pair. The father's are on light ground; the son's float on black. Both fill the picture edge to edge with humans, animals, spirits and hybrid beings, plus activist text on Indigenous rights and environmental destruction. Mythic creatures in the son's work are violent and sexual.
claims: The pairing shows an evolution in visual language from father to son.
Kissick wrote that their weirdness, not their identity, is what makes them great.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.venue_room: Italian Pavilion, far end of the Arsenale (cavernous warehouse space)
works.title: Due Qui / To Hear
works.medium_line: Sound and architecture installation: scaffolding, organ machine, organ pipe, pool; music by Caterina Barbieri, Kali Malone, Gavin Bryars
works.what_you_see: A long hand-made wooden bass organ pipe runs most of the length of the floor and gives a low hum. Through a doorway a scaffolding maze about fifty metres long carries an automated organ-like machine that pushes slow ambient music through its pipes. At the centre is a round pool of pulsing water. In the garden a choral piece by Gavin Bryars and his son plays from the trees. A second work, Pensive Bodhisattva on A Flat, lays a bodhisattva statue on a flat wooden column that turns out to be an organ pipe sounding a drone in A flat.
nonvisual: sound: low drone, ambient organ lament, choral piece from trees
water: pulsing pool
claims: The curator writes that listening is a form of attention to others.
Kissick: a rare utopian space not reducible to social messaging.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.title: Moré Moré (Leaky): Variations
works.medium_line: Kinetic and sound installation: fruit, electrodes, speakers, leaking tubes, faucets, buckets, found objects
works.what_you_see: Polished wooden tables hold rotting fruit wired by electrodes to speakers and lights. Elsewhere, wobbling contraptions of tubes, faucets, buckets and found objects catch artificial leaks, copying the makeshift fixes of the Tokyo subway. It looks more like a laboratory or food-processing plant than a gallery. Fruit slowly decays through the run.
nonvisual: sound: moisture in the fruit modulates ambient tones
scent: the smell of decay fills the pavilion
light: flicker driven by the fruit
claims: The leaks are never fully fixed; the futile fixes show human creativity.
The decay cycle refers to the Buddhist nine stages of decay.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.title: the space in which to place me
works.medium_line: Paintings, totemic sculptures, beadwork and textile garments, multichannel film (She Never Dances Alone), live performances
works.what_you_see: Bold colour fills the pavilion: large geometric paintings and totem-like sculptures decorated with beads and fabric. The pieces serve as stages for performers at set hours. A multi-channel film, She Never Dances Alone, runs inside.
nonvisual: performance: performers use the art as stage at scheduled times
claims: First Native American solo artist at the US pavilion.
Weaves intertribal aesthetics with European modernism and centres Indigenous communities.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.title: Listening All Night to the Rain
works.medium_line: Eight-part multimedia film and sound installation
works.dimensions: Total running time about five hours
works.what_you_see: Eight rooms, called cantos, show films on several screens at once. Archive footage, newly shot film and still images interlock with text. A quotation above one doorway reads that boats are open and sailed for everyone (Edouard Glissant). Viewers cannot take in all of it in one visit.
nonvisual: sound: water recordings, voices and music form the structure
claims: Listening is positioned as activism and as a way to know the world (acoustemology).
Links migrant diasporas, ecological harm and colonial histories.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.venue_room: German Pavilion, Giardini (plus La Certosa island)
works.title: Thresholds
works.medium_line: Earth monolith, spaceship sculpture, mist and light, performance, film
works.what_you_see: The pavilion exterior is banked with soil up to the high windows; inside an earthen monolith stands at the centre. Rays of light pour through pumped-in mist from the high windows, and a sculptural spaceship hovers in a side room. Performers move through the spaces. A queue of visitors formed from opening week.
nonvisual: performance: live actors
sound: a voice (Louis Chude-Sokei) greets visitors
claims: Built as a monument to forgotten working men; refers to Mondtag's grandfather who migrated from Anatolia in the 1960s.
Thresholds are liminal spaces between places and times.
works.photo_notes: Described as filmic: rays of light through pumped-in mist and a hovering spaceship.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.artist: CATPC (Cercle d'Art des Travailleurs de Plantation Congolaise) with Renzo Martens, curated by Hicham Khalidi
works.title: The International Celebration of Blasphemy and the Sacred
works.medium_line: Cocoa-covered sculptures and installation
works.what_you_see: Vivid sculptures covered in cocoa fill the pavilion. A strong smell of cocoa meets visitors at the door. The material comes from land once planted by Unilever.
nonvisual: scent: strong cocoa smell
claims: Sales of the sculptures fund buying back plantation land where the artists and families have worked.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.venue_room: Benin Pavilion (curated by Azu Nwagbogu), Arsenale
works.title: Àṣẹ
works.medium_line: Dome of jerrycans
works.what_you_see: A tall dome made of jerrycans (fuel canisters) with the spouts pointing down, as though about to pour. Visitors can step inside. A faint scent of incense gives the dome a sacred quality.
nonvisual: scent: faint incense
claims: Jerrycans form a dome visitors can enter; incense lends it a sacred quality.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.venue_room: Arsenale, under the arches facing the Grand Canal
works.artist: Claire Fontaine (Fulvia Carnevale and James Thornhill)
works.title: Stranieri Ovunque (Autoritratto), Foreigners Everywhere (Self-portrait)
works.medium_line: Double-sided wall or window-mounted neon, framework, transformers, cables and fittings, dimensions and colours variable
works.what_you_see: A rainbow of neon words hangs under the arches of the Arsenale looking out to the water, and glitters in its reflections. It is the first work visitors see together with Shonibare's Refugee Astronaut VIII. The slogan has been made in many languages since 2004.
nonvisual: light: neon glow reflected on the water
claims: The phrase is the source of the Biennale's title, a homage to a Turin anti-racist collective.
works.photo_notes: Described as a glittering rainbow of neon reflected in the water below.

works.exhibition: 60th Venice Biennale: Stranieri Ovunque / Foreigners Everywhere
works.title: Don't miss the cue!
works.medium_line: Suzani textiles, screens with AI-generated patterns
works.what_you_see: Traditional suzani embroidery hangs beside screens where AI generates new suzani-like patterns. A peacock motif morphs into sewing machines; a teapot motif turns into a 'girl dinner' image. The installation sits in a former House of Culture style space.
claims: Examines women's craft traditions through machine-made variants.

works.exhibition: Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing
works.title: The Last Safe Abortion
works.medium_line: Collage of printed photographs
works.dimensions: About 2,700 images; fills a gallery wall
works.what_you_see: A huge wall is covered edge to edge with about 2,700 colour prints. The pictures show ordinary days in abortion clinics and protests after Roe v. Wade was overturned. Short blocks of text appear among them. The rows are arranged like a tapestry with warp and weft.
claims: Makes an abstract issue into a lived experience of time, money and logistics.
A critic found it persuasive without changing anyone's mind; it won over viewers through sheer accumulation.
references: clinic archives in the Midwest and South
works.photo_notes: Installation views show a dense colour grid covering a large white wall.

works.exhibition: Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing
works.title: deepest ocean, what we do not know, we might see?
works.medium_line: Acrylic medium and pigment poured on plastic sheets; mixed media; suspended
works.what_you_see: A whole gallery of translucent painted sheets that hang from the ceiling or lean on the wall like sails. The sheets are made from layers of poured acrylic and hold bits of pistachio shells, nylon curtain mesh, produce-bag netting and shredded mail. Silhouettes of visitors show through.
claims: The pieces work like records of a journey taken with materials.
works.photo_notes: Described as a gossamer surface that lets silhouettes and movement show through.

works.exhibition: Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing
works.title: Ruins of Empire II or The Earth Swallows the Master's House
works.medium_line: Earth and steel
works.what_you_see: The north facade of the White House, rebuilt in sod and steel, leans and sinks into the ground on the open terrace. Hairline cracks cross the earth. An upside-down American flag flaps beside it.
claims: All empires end; the earth swallows the master's house.

works.exhibition: Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing
works.title: Paloma Blanca Deja Volar / White Dove Let Us Fly
works.medium_line: Modified amber, volcanic stone, pigeon wings, ceramic, cloth, archival documents, found objects
works.what_you_see: A monolithic block of amber stands in front of a sunlit window. Warmth slowly melts, cracks and shifts it. Through the amber you can see suspended documents, volcanic stone, pigeon wings, cloth, grasses, leaves and tree limbs, like objects frozen in a river of resin.
claims: Slow change in the amber stands in for how memory and trauma shift in the body.
Embedded papers concern white solidarity activists and the Central American peace movement.
references: Central American Peace and Solidarity Movement
works.photo_notes: Described as an amber-coloured block with objects suspended inside, in front of a window.

works.exhibition: Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing
works.title: Daughters: Reverence
works.medium_line: Clay, steel, grout, twine, pine and hide
works.what_you_see: Four rough-surfaced humanoid figures stand like compass points, turned inward, with hollow eyes lifted upwards. They are decorated with twine and beads and carry the look of Pueblo ceramic tradition. The figures read as both ancestors and future ancestors.
claims: Heals the damage of the postmodern and postcolonial era, in the artist's words.
A matrilineal lineage connected to the universe.
references: Pueblo ceramic tradition (mother, grandmother and great-grandmother)

works.exhibition: Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing
works.venue_room: Sixth floor or gallery with musical works
works.title: TEMPO RUBATO (STOLEN TIME)
works.medium_line: Modified player piano, audio and LED lighting system
works.what_you_see: A player piano whose keys move with no player and no music: the performance has been silenced so only the clicks and mechanics are heard and lit, amplified through a custom sound and light rig. Visitors watch the machine's inner works rather than hear a song.
nonvisual: sound: amplified mechanical noise of the piano action, not the melody
claims: The piece asks how labour and performance become intellectual property.
Won the Whitney's Bucksbaum Award.

works.exhibition: Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing
works.venue_room: Fifth floor, visible from the street
works.title: we must stop imagining apocalypse/genocide + we must imagine liberation
works.medium_line: Red neon and steel
works.what_you_see: Red neon sentences in a protest-sign style are mounted on steel in the window. The tubes flicker and, as they do, spell out 'Free Palestine'. Another text calls on viewers to stop predicting apocalypses and fascist governments, and to imagine routes towards liberation. It can be seen from the street.
nonvisual: light: flickering red neon
claims: Challenges Euro-Western fascination with dystopia; the Free Palestine message was hidden until the press preview.

works.exhibition: Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing
works.venue_room: Gallery next to Weston's glass installation
works.medium_line: Paintings
works.what_you_see: Paintings of shutters, boards and window frames that crash against each other. Openings appear to promise a view but are filled with a block of muted colour. They are hung beside Charisse Weston's smoked glass parallelograms, whose angles echo them.
claims: The only dead artist in the main section; ARTnews called her paintings a possible key to the show.

works.exhibition: Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing
works.title: How Many Ways Can You Disappear
works.medium_line: Found Maine lobster traps, pot warp, buoys, rope cast in salt, resin
works.what_you_see: A tangle of multicoloured rope lies on the floor with found buoys hung over it. A rope made of salt hangs from the pieces. The sculpture is installed without barriers, so visitors walk right up to it.
claims: Wall text links salt to the ancient trade of salt for enslaved people.
Kissick cited this as a case where meaning lives only in the label.

works.exhibition: Whitney Biennial 2026
works.venue_room: Fifth floor, outside the elevators (first work seen)
works.title: Kong Play
works.medium_line: Ceramic, painted
works.dimensions: 100 objects on a low two-tier plinth
works.what_you_see: A hundred bulbous ceramic copies of a dog's chew toy sit on a low two-tiered plinth, each painted a different hue. Drawings nearby show the blind artist in everyday and fantastical scenes with their guide dog. It reads as a shrine to the dead dog.
claims: A tribute to the artist's guide dog London; envisions an afterlife of play.
Blurs the hierarchy between humans and animals.

works.exhibition: Whitney Biennial 2026
works.title: Requiem for the Insects
works.medium_line: Sound, scent, sculpture and painting
works.what_you_see: A room installation that combines paintings, sculpture and glass megaphones that play insect sounds. A scent drifts through the space.
nonvisual: sound: insect calls through glass megaphones
scent: part of the installation
claims: The artist wants viewers to pause and engage with natural languages through sound and smell, instead of 'I know that, next'.

works.exhibition: Whitney Biennial 2026
works.venue_room: Sixth floor near terrace (some reports say fifth floor)
works.artist: José Maceda, recreated by Aki Onda
works.title: Ugnayan (Music for Twenty Radio Stations)
works.medium_line: Installation of 20 radios playing simultaneously
works.what_you_see: Twenty radios stand together and play twenty parts of one composition at the same time. Documentation of the 1974 broadcast and its promotion by the Marcos regime sits alongside.
nonvisual: sound: twenty simultaneous parts for voice and Indigenous instruments
claims: Raises whether art can ever be separated from politics; the original was transmitted on 20 Manila radio stations at once.

works.exhibition: Whitney Biennial 2026
works.title: Monument (Altadena)
works.medium_line: Glass brick reconstruction of a fireplace and chimney
works.what_you_see: A ghostly replica of her house's fireplace and chimney, built in glass brick on the open terrace. It is the only part of her Altadena home left after the Eaton fire.
claims: A monument to grief for a home lost.

works.exhibition: Whitney Biennial 2026
works.artist_lives: New York (self-styled street queen); died (date not stated in source)
works.title: Ethyl (Altar)
works.medium_line: Jewelry, matchbooks, pins, textile; plastic, metal and ceramic objects; postcards, photographs, handmade feather butterfly, mask with glitter, coins, makeup compact; works by Peter Hujar, Thomas Lanigan-Schmidt, Uzi Parnes
works.what_you_see: A crowded altar-like assemblage of hoarded personal things: jewellery, matchbooks, pins, glitter masks, postcards, photographs and containers of ephemera. Each altar remembers a friend or figure of New York's queer counterculture. Several altars are shown close together.
claims: Built through years of caring for chosen family during the AIDS epidemic.

works.exhibition: Whitney Biennial 2026
works.artist: Carmen de Monteflores (paintings) and Andrea Fraser (wax sculptures)
works.title: Four Women
works.medium_line: Shaped canvases, paired with hyperrealist wax sculptures of sleeping toddlers (Fraser, 2024)
works.what_you_see: Three boldly coloured shaped canvases of intertwined nude couples and groups, painted in the late 1960s, hang near five lifelike wax toddlers asleep in plexiglass cases. The wax is a type that never hardens.
materials: acrylic or oil on shaped canvas
claims: The pairing shows how a mother gave up art when her youngest child (the artist's daughter) was born.
references: art world's lack of support for mothers

works.exhibition: Whitney Biennial 2026
works.title: Sunflower Cam (also Angel Cam, Bunny Cam)
works.medium_line: Ceramic sculptures with pinhole apertures; ceramic frames with photographic prints
works.what_you_see: Freestanding ceramic sculptures that look like amoebas or sea anemones have small holes and work as pinhole cameras. Some were placed in the New Mexico desert, and their blurry images hang in a grid of mismatched ceramic frames.
claims: Connects ceramic and photographic processes: both involve a change of state that the maker does not see.

works.exhibition: Unravel: The Power and Politics of Textiles in Art
works.title: Quipu Austral
works.medium_line: Unspun dyed wool, installation
works.what_you_see: A forest of long, slender lengths of unspun wool, dyed in bright colours and knotted at the top, hangs from the ceiling and stirs when visitors pass. The knots echo the Andean quipu.
claims: The knots form a system of writing that links the makers to the cosmos (curator tour text).
During the show she kept the work in and pinned a solidarity letter beside it.

works.exhibition: Unravel: The Power and Politics of Textiles in Art
works.title: Blood in the Grass
works.medium_line: Tapestry
works.what_you_see: A colourful hand-woven anti-Vietnam war tapestry with strong colour and texture.
claims: Protest tapestry that connects domestic weaving to political comment.

works.exhibition: Unravel: The Power and Politics of Textiles in Art
works.venue_room: Barbican Art Gallery, Fabric of Everyday Life
works.title: Family Treasures
works.medium_line: Yarn bundles of cherished items
works.what_you_see: A group of brightly coloured bundles of fabric and yarn, each wrapped around items given by family members. They are arranged as a small field of soft sculptures.
claims: Challenges the domestic and decorative image of textiles.

works.exhibition: Unravel: The Power and Politics of Textiles in Art
works.title: american Juju for the Tapestry of Truth
works.medium_line: Patchwork tapestries with blood or ground residue
works.what_you_see: Patchwork cloths: one carries blood from a woman killed in Panama City, another was laid on the New York street where Eric Garner was killed. One piece was absent on a reviewer's visit.
claims: Material protest against forgetting violent death.

works.exhibition: Hyundai Commission, Tate Modern Turbine Hall 2023
works.title: Behind the Red Moon
works.medium_line: Hangings of crushed bottle tops and copper wire; black wall; metal pools
works.what_you_see: Act I is a red-and-yellow billowing sail on the ramp, with red caps forming a blood-moon disc. Act II is a layered group of hanging figures made of thin bottle-top seals wired into a net, which merge into the circle of the Earth when seen from the bridge. Act III is a black wall from floor to ceiling with metal 'waves' at its base.
nonvisual: sound: soundscape by Peter Adjaye
claims: Connected to transatlantic trade in sugar, rum and people.
Breaking is not destruction but a necessity for reforming.

works.exhibition: Hyundai Commission, Tate Modern Turbine Hall 2024
works.title: Open Wound
works.medium_line: Kinetic installation: motorised turbine, silicone hoses, steel frames, scaffolding netting, chains, viscous liquid
works.dimensions: Turbine about 8 m long and over 3 tonnes; 49 chains; skins grew from 98 to 152
works.what_you_see: A slowly rotating turbine hangs from a ceiling crane and sloshes dark pink liquid through fleshy silicone tubes on to pale fabric 'skins'. The skins drape over bent steel frames and are then dried on racks and hauled up on chains. Technicians in hi-vis move them. Cladding was stripped from the bridge to expose wiring.
materials: liquid of water, methyl cellulose, pigment and aspirin
nonvisual: sound: dripping liquid
performance: technicians work during opening hours
claims: A factory-like body: soft organic forms against rigid machinery.
Lee says being moved is the strongest thing art can do.

works.exhibition: Hyundai Commission, Tate Modern Turbine Hall 2025
works.title: Goavve-Geabbil
works.medium_line: Reindeer hides bound by electrical cables; maze structure; sound and scent
works.what_you_see: Reindeer hides are tightly bound by power cables in a tall hanging sculpture. Beside it is a maze-like structure modelled on the inside of a reindeer's nose, with wall carvings from family earmarks and seats covered in reindeer hide where visitors listen to stories through headphones.
nonvisual: scent: lichen, shoegrass, reindeer milk and the artist's breast milk, plus the fear-scent of reindeer
sound: joik and landscape recordings, stories from Sami knowledge keepers
claims: Energy as a sacred life-force sustained by reciprocity.
Presents Sami science as hard knowledge.

works.exhibition: 58th Carnegie International: Is it morning for you yet?
works.title: Eye Eye
works.medium_line: Pigment made from soil on copper-coloured painting
works.dimensions: Large; greets visitors in the lobby
works.what_you_see: A striking copper-toned abstract painting meets visitors in the museum lobby. Its pigment comes from soil of land she recently came to own in Canada.
claims: Asks what private ownership of land means for an Indigenous person on a reservation held by the Crown.
